notes: Maritime limitation appeal; charterer liability scope and 1976 Convention analysis are clear in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Charterer limitation of liability for cargo explosion damage

statutes_considered.title: Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims 1976

key_facts: The container ship CMA DJAKARTA suffered an explosion caused by bleaching powder in two containers shipped in breach of the time charterparty.
Arbitrators held charterers liable for about US$26.6m repair costs and related declaratory awards.
The appeal concerned whether charterers could limit liability under the 1976 Convention as incorporated by the Merchant Shipping Act 1995.
David Steel J had held that a charterer may limit only when acting qua shipowner in activities usually associated with ownership or operation of the vessel.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from an arbitration award on the scope of a charterer's right to limit liability for maritime claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; charterers may limit only in respect of cargo-related claims and not for damage to the ship or consequential loss; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under the 1976 Convention as enacted by the Merchant Shipping Act 1995, a charterer's right to limit is not confined to acts done strictly qua shipowner, but in this case limitation applies only to cargo claims and not to claims for damage to the ship or consequential loss arising from such damage; the capacity in which a charterer acts is primarily a question of fact.
legal_issues: Whether a time charterer may limit liability under the 1976 Convention
Meaning of 'shipowner' and 'charterer' in Article 1 of the Convention
Which categories of owner claims against a charterer are subject to limitation
Whether the case should be remitted to the arbitrators on limitation issues
linked_authorities: The Aegean Sea [1998] 2 Lloyd's Rep 39
The Tychy [1999] 2 Lloyd's Rep 11
The Francesca [1985] 1 Lloyd's Rep 399
Monroe Brothers v Ryan [1935] AC 129
CMA CGM S.A. v Classica Shipping Co Ltd [2003] 2 Lloyd's Rep 50

confidence.notes: Outcome, Convention articles, and limitation categories are explicit. Some linked House of Lords authorities are cited historically but not central to the ratio.

notes: Winding-up petition restraint on disputed CHP contract debt; genuine dispute analysis straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Restraining winding-up petition over disputed CHP contract debt
key_facts: Dalkia served a statutory demand for £3,648,367.29 after terminating a long-term CHP energy supply and financing contract with Celtech International Ltd.
Celtech operates a paper mill and disputed both Dalkia's right to terminate and the sums claimed under the Principal Agreement and amendments.
Dalkia later accepted the statutory demand figure was wrong and claimed over £4.6m on revised calculations.
Celtech applied to restrain presentation of a winding-up petition based on the disputed debt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for injunction restraining presentation of a winding-up petition based on a statutory demand.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction granted restraining Dalkia from presenting a winding-up petition based on the statutory demand or other Agreement claims unless supported by a judgment in Dalkia's favour.
enrichment.ratio: Where there is a genuine dispute on substantial grounds as to whether a creditor was entitled to terminate a contract and as to the amount due, and a potential cross-claim may exceed the debt, it is inappropriate to allow a winding-up petition to proceed on the disputed sum; a repudiatory breach and damages claim raised late cannot substitute for a petition based on an unquantified disputed debt.
legal_issues: Whether there was a genuine dispute barring a winding-up petition
Whether Dalkia was entitled to terminate under clause 14.4 of the Principal Agreement
Whether sums claimed under clause 15.4 were due and enforceable
Whether alleged repudiatory breach by Celtech supported a petition

confidence.notes: Core insolvency dispute principles and outcome are clear. Penalty clause arguments were not decided.

notes: Versailles Group fraud claim heard in private; fortification and security for costs refusals are clear but merits evidence is limited in the public judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Versailles fraud claim: fortification and security refused
key_facts: Sinclair Investment Holdings claimed about £2.35m invested with Trading Partners Ltd was misapplied through the Versailles Group, including companies controlled by Mr Carlton Cushnie.
Mr Cushnie gave an undertaking not to dispose of a French property (L'Ecossaise) pending trial; Sinclair gave a cross-undertaking in damages backed by FHC.
Mr Cushnie applied for fortification of the cross-undertaking and for security for costs before any defence had been served.
Parallel criminal proceedings concerning Versailles Group accounts were ongoing at the time of the hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim applications for fortification of a cross-undertaking in damages and for security for costs in a trust and fraud claim.
enrichment.outcome: Fortification of the cross-undertaking refused; application for security for costs refused as premature.
enrichment.ratio: Fortification of a cross-undertaking requires a sufficient demonstrated risk of loss from the restraint; thin and late business-plan evidence did not establish that risk in respect of a single-property undertaking. Security for costs should not be ordered before defence when the claim shape and merits are unclear and the application appears tactical.
legal_issues: Whether the cross-undertaking in damages should be fortified
Whether sufficient risk of loss was shown from restraint over L'Ecossaise
Whether security for costs should be ordered against an overseas impecunious claimant
Whether CPR 3.1(5) sanctions were warranted for without-notice freezing order procedure
linked_authorities: Staines v Walsh [2003] EWHC 1486
De Bry v Fitzgerald [1990] 1 WLR 540
Bhimji v Chatwani [1992] BCLC 387
Keary Developments Ltd v Tarmac Construction Ltd [1995] 3 All ER 534
In re DPR Futures Ltd [1989] 1 WLR 778

confidence.notes: Interim procedural outcomes are clear, but the hearing was in private and underlying fraud merits are only lightly described.

notes: Complex immigration judicial review with multiple grounds; proportionality and delay holding is clear but rule 301 analysis is lengthy.

enrichment.short_title: Family reunion leave and Article 8 proportionality delay
key_facts: Four Ugandan children sought entry clearance to join their sponsor in the UK; two were biological children and two were raised as her own.
The sponsor had been granted exceptional leave to remain after an asylum claim; entry clearance was refused in 2000.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal against an adjudicator's dismissal of the children's appeals.
Substantial delay by the Secretary of State in deciding the sponsor's status was argued to affect Article 8 proportionality.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review granted; IAT decision quashed and remitted for reconsideration on proportionality and delay; Secretary of State succeeded on rule 301 interpretation.
enrichment.ratio: The IAT erred in holding there was no arguable appeal on proportionality where culpable delay in immigration decision-making was a relevant Article 8 factor not properly considered; however rule 301 did not apply to these children's applications and the sponsor's de facto parental relationship did not bring them within that provision.
legal_issues: Whether rule 301 Immigration Rules applied to the children's applications
Meaning of 'parent' for family reunion purposes
Whether delay by the Secretary of State affected Article 8 proportionality
Whether the IAT should have granted leave to appeal
linked_authorities: Shala v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 233
Attafuah v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2002] UK IAT 05922
In re S (Minors) (Care Order: Implementation of Care Plan) [2002] WLR 720

confidence.notes: Final order and proportionality holding are explicit. Multiple grounds and rule construction are dense; individual child outcomes may differ on remittal.

notes: Aircraft bailee liability and insurance representation dispute; quantum and outcome clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Aircraft bailee liability after fatal Newmarket crash
key_facts: Oxford Aviation Services owned a Piper Seneca aircraft hired to Godolphin Management for jockey transport.
The aircraft crashed on take-off at Newmarket Racecourse in June 2000, killing the pilot and injuring passengers including Frankie Dettori.
Godolphin admitted bailee status and inability to disprove pilot negligence but alleged Oxford had contractually agreed to provide comprehensive insurance cover.
Oxford had no insurance covering Godolphin's use; the parties' oral arrangements over two trial aircraft were disputed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of liability and quantum in a bailee's claim for aircraft loss and related losses after a fatal crash.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for Oxford in the sum of £308,760 with interest; Godolphin's counterclaim dismissed; declaration granted as to indemnity for further claims.
enrichment.ratio: A bailee liable for loss caused by negligent piloting cannot escape liability by an unproved oral representation that the owner would provide comprehensive third-party insurance; without a signed hire agreement or documentary support, alleged insurance arrangements inconsistent with Oxford's commercial practice fail.
legal_issues: Whether Godolphin was liable as bailee for the destroyed aircraft
Whether an oral contract or representation obliged Oxford to insure Godolphin's use
Quantum of loss including replacement value, hire charges and mitigation
Whether survey fees were recoverable as damages
linked_authorities: Collier v Stamco (Stainless Steel) Ltd [1990] 1 WLR 922
Henthorn v Fraser [1892] 2 Ch 27

confidence.notes: Liability finding, damages breakdown and declaration are explicit in the judgment.

notes: Second retrial appeal on building contract novation and forgery; outcome and new evidence refusal are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Building contract novation and forged signature appeal
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Daly contracted with Middlesex Design and Build Ltd for a home extension but allege an oral novation to Mr Sheikh personally.
Mr Daly paid about £70,000 in cash after Mr Sheikh requested payment to him rather than the company.
Works were defective and partially collapsed; the Dalys claimed about £65,250 plus loss of amenity.
After two trials on a preliminary issue, Mr Sheikh sought a second retrial relying on new handwriting expert evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal of a second retrial of a preliminary issue, with an application to admit fresh handwriting evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Fresh evidence application refused and appeal dismissed; freezing order to continue; appellant ordered to pay respondents' costs.
enrichment.ratio: Fresh expert evidence discovered after two trials will not be admitted where it could and should have been obtained earlier through proper scrutiny of disclosed documents; on the novation issue the court had already chosen between conflicting witness credibility and further retrial would not be justified.
legal_issues: Whether fresh handwriting evidence should be admitted on appeal
Whether an oral novation transferred the building contract from MDB to Mr Sheikh
Whether a second retrial of the preliminary issue was warranted
Whether the freezing order should remain in place
linked_authorities: Ladd v Marshall [1954] 3 All ER 745
Daly v Sheikh [2002] EWHC 846

confidence.notes: Appeal outcome, fresh evidence refusal and costs order are explicit. Underlying forgery finding rests on prior trial judgments.

notes: Solicitor negligence in goat-farming litigation; damages and indemnities clearly quantified.

key_facts: Mr and Mrs Browning bought a goat farming business from Mr Gilham and counterclaimed for Johne's disease losses potentially exceeding £120,000.
Their solicitors Brachers failed to serve witness statements and expert evidence before a unless order, barring the counterclaim.
The counterclaim was dismissed in December 1996; the Brownings later sued Gilham's estate and then Brachers for negligence.
Brachers admitted some negligence but disputed the full extent and quantum of loss.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a professional negligence claim against solicitors for failure to prepare and pursue a counterclaim in county court litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants succeeded; damages of £51,357 awarded with interest; Brachers ordered to indemnify claimants for three quarters of Gilham action costs and for costs of the action against Mrs Gilham.
enrichment.ratio: Solicitors who negligently fail to progress and prepare a counterclaim are liable for the loss of a real chance of success assessed generously at trial; where the original action would likely have succeeded overall, the negligent firm must indemnify the client for costs risks and core damages flowing from the lost opportunity.
legal_issues: Whether Brachers were negligent in conduct of the Gilham litigation
What the claimants would have recovered at a notional trial
Whether implied terms under the Sale of Goods Act 1979 were breached
Quantum of damages, interest and indemnities for related costs orders

Keefe v Isle of Man Steam Packet Co [1990] 2 AC 549
Jaura v Ahmed [2002] EWCA Civ 210

confidence.notes: Negligence findings, damages figure and indemnity orders are explicit. Some notional trial findings involve evaluative judgment.

notes: Security for costs and conditions on permission to appeal in large fraud litigation; orders clearly specified.

enrichment.short_title: Security for costs and conditions on fraud appeal
key_facts: Claimants obtained substantial judgments against offshore defendants Mora and Chascona after repeated non-compliance with freezing and unless orders.
Etherton J dismissed applications to set aside the judgments; permission to appeal was granted on discretion issues.
The litigation was funded by Mr Paolo Cavazza, beneficial owner of the defendant companies.
Claimants sought security for appeal costs and payment into court of past assessed costs as conditions of permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for security for costs and for conditions to be attached to permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants ordered to provide £600,000 for past costs and £450,000 security for appeal costs as conditions of permission; partial security orders made under the claimants' draft order.
enrichment.ratio: Where defendants have repeatedly flouted court orders, judgment has already been entered against them, an appeal is funded by a wealthy non-party financier and there is no risk of stifling, the court may impose substantial security for past and appeal costs as a condition of permission to appeal.
legal_issues: Whether security for costs should be ordered for the appeal
Whether conditions should attach to permission to appeal requiring payment of past costs
Effect of repeated breach of court orders and unless orders
Relevance of third-party funding by Mr Cavazza
linked_authorities: Olatawura v Abilowe [2002] EWCA Civ 998
Contract Facilities Ltd v The Estate of Rees [2003] EWCA Civ 1105
CIBC Mellon Trust Co v Stolzenberg [2001] EWCA Civ 2065

notes: Commercial Court construction of ACAS mediation clause; strike-out outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: ACAS mediation clause not an arbitration agreement
key_facts: Flight Training and IFTE entered Heads of Terms to collaborate on supplying a Boeing 747 anti-terrorist training mock-up to the Saudi Royal Guard.
Article XI provided that disputes be submitted to ACAS and that legal fees be paid by the party not prevailing at mediation.
Flight Training applied under section 18 for appointment of an arbitrator; IFTE applied to strike out for lack of a valid arbitration agreement.
ACAS does not provide mediation for commercial disputes of this nature.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court applications under section 18 Arbitration Act 1996 and to strike out for absence of an arbitration agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Defendant's application succeeded; no agreement to refer the dispute to arbitration; claimant's section 18 application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A dispute resolution clause referring disputes to ACAS and expressly to mediation, with costs consequences tied to prevailing at mediation, is an agreement to mediate and not an arbitration agreement within sections 5 and 6 of the Arbitration Act 1996; reference to mediation in the operative sentence is inconsistent with an intention to arbitrate.
legal_issues: Whether Article XI constituted an arbitration agreement
Construction of a clause referring disputes to ACAS
Effect of the second sentence on costs of mediation
Whether section 18 directions should be made
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
Cable & Wireless plc v IBM United Kingdom Ltd [2002] 2 All ER (Comm) 1041
Dunnett v Railtrack plc [2002] 1 WLR 2434
Prenn v Simmonds [1971] 1 WLR 1381
North Eastern Railway Co v Lord Hastings [1900] AC 260

confidence.notes: Issue, construction analysis and strike-out outcome are directly addressed in the judgment.

notes: Embassy Court leasehold maintenance dispute; benefit-and-burden principle and appeal dismissal clear.

enrichment.short_title: Embassy Court leasehold maintenance and benefit-and-burden
key_facts: Embassy Court is a landmark 1930s Brighton seafront block that fell into disrepair under Portvale Holdings' ownership.
Bluestorm Ltd became freeholder after Portvale dissolved its landlord company following adverse judgments.
Portvale remained a major leaseholder but refused to pay maintenance contributions despite lease obligations.
Bluestorm counterclaimed for maintenance contributions; Portvale argued Bluestorm had disclaimed its repairing obligations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a 10-day trial on leasehold service charge and maintenance contribution disputes.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tenant counterclaim for specific performance of lessor's obligations dismissed on benefit-and-burden grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tenant has evinced a fixed intention not to be bound by its obligation to pay maintenance contributions, it cannot claim the benefit of the landlord's repairing covenant; on the express terms of these leases the benefit-and-burden principle prevents recovery where the tenant has disentitled itself by non-performance.
legal_issues: Whether Bluestorm was in breach of repairing obligations
Whether Portvale was obliged to pay maintenance contributions
Application of the benefit-and-burden principle in long leases
Causation of other tenants' failure to contribute
linked_authorities: Yorkbrook Investments Ltd v Batten [1986] 1 WLR 457
Halsall v Brizell [1957] Ch 169
Tito v Waddell (No 2) [1977] Ch 106
Wardlaw v Bonnington Castings Ltd [1956] AC 613
